headline: mixed
texts: Some of this topic is solid and some is not yet. The pattern below shows which ideas held and which still wobble. Varicose veins mixes mechanism, eponyms and a changed treatment order, so a few weak spots are normal. Start with the review cards listed first; they target your most important misses.
Mostly there on the commonest vein, site and type, with some slips or guesses. Keep the qualifier: GSV and SFJ reflux are the commonest, not the only pattern. CEAP C2 is 3 mm or more standing.
Your flow-direction reasoning is partly right. State the normal direction first, then ask what reflux reverses. The normal calf pump lowers pressure; with reflux it fails to fall.

Anatomy is partly in place. Anchor the GSV as medial, in front of the malleolus, ending in the femoral vein, and the SSV as lateral, behind the malleolus, ending in the popliteal vein. Perforators run Cockett, Boyd, Dodd, Hunter going up.
The nerve pairing or stripping limit is only partly secure. Link each nerve to its companion vein: saphenous with GSV, sural with SSV. The GSV is stripped only to just below the knee.
Ulcer site or CEAP numbers are partly secure. Tie each number to a sign: C4 skin change, C5 healed ulcer, C6 active ulcer. The venous ulcer sits just above the medial malleolus.

You partly separate the Brodie-Trendelenburg and Perthes tests. Go by the maneuver: compress the junction and stand (SFJ), or tourniquet and walk (deep vein patency). Re-check the filling patterns too.
The deep-vein check before surgery is partly secure. Positive Perthes or an occluded deep system means no stripping or ligation, because superficial veins are carrying the collateral outflow.
Mostly right on investigations. Hold the ladder: hand-held Doppler detects junctional reflux, duplex maps reflux, perforators and deep patency, venography is only for complex deep disease.

The treatment ladder is partly secure. Current first-line is endothermal ablation, then foam sclerotherapy, then open surgery; PYQs expected Trendelenburg with stripping. Stockings suit pregnancy, after treatment, or unsuitability for intervention.

Sclerotherapy is partly secure. Foam displaces blood and works better in larger veins; liquid suits telangiectasias and reticular veins. STS is the classic key; polidocanol is an accepted modern agent.
The ulcer-leg sequence is partly secure. Measure ABPI first; with ABPI under 0.8, hold compression and look for arterial disease. Multilayer compression is the mainstay once it is safe.
Partly there on varix versus femoral hernia. Both have a cough impulse; the discriminators are the fluid thrill on tapping and disappearance on lying down.

You chose the old PYQ key (Trendelenburg with stripping) first, then switched. Credit that. Under exam pressure the 'SFJ incompetence means operation' association pulls back. Rule: 'current' or 'first-line' means ablation; 'classic' means the operation.

You first reached for hand-held Doppler or venography, then moved to duplex. Keep the ladder in mind, because familiar test names tempt under time pressure: Doppler detects, duplex maps, venography is for deep disease.

You swapped the Perthes and Brodie-Trendelenburg tests at first, then sorted them. Credit that, but the names are easy to flip again under pressure. Anchor to the maneuver: compress the junction and stand, versus tourniquet and walk.

You first called filling under compression SFJ incompetence, then fixed it. The compression blocks the junction, so filling that still occurs must enter elsewhere. That reasoning is easy to drop in a hurry.
You first merged the Trendelenburgs, then separated them. Under exam pressure the eponym alone may pull you again; read the noun that follows it.

You first merged the two saphenous veins, then separated them. Both start at the dorsal venous arch, which is why they blur. Anchor by medial or lateral: GSV to the femoral vein, SSV to the popliteal vein.
You first swapped the saphenous and sural nerves, then corrected. Under pressure, go vein first: saphenous nerve with the GSV, sural nerve with the SSV.
You first took stripping to the ankle, then changed. Your 'remove the whole vein' model is the one that returns in a rush; the limit is just below the knee because of the saphenous nerve.
You first misplaced the perforators, then ordered them. Keep the ankle-to-thigh walk; Dodd and Hunter are thigh, Cockett is ankle, Boyd just below the knee.
You first let perforator valves pass blood deep to superficial, then corrected. Always state the healthy direction before asking what reflux reverses.
You first said walking raises venous pressure, then fixed it. Symptoms worsen on standing, which tempts a backward mechanism. The normal pump lowers pressure; with reflux it fails to fall.
You first muddled a CEAP number or class, then corrected. Numbers slip under pressure; hold signs: below 1 mm telangiectasia, 3 mm or more varicose, C5 healed, C6 active.
You first went to compression for the ulcer, then put ABPI first. Compression is the mainstay, so it is the answer the mind jumps to; ask what could make it harmful.
You first treated a positive Perthes as reassuring, then reversed. Ask where the blood goes when the superficial veins are removed; if the deep system is blocked, they are collaterals.
You first read 'most common' as 'only', then corrected. In 'which is NOT' wording, an absolute claim is the one to distrust.
You first used foam for telangiectasias or liquid for trunks, then corrected. Foam displaces blood in a large lumen, which is why it works better in larger veins.
You first rejected polidocanol, then accepted both. If only one is listed, pick it; if both are listed, both are valid.
You first called a saphena varix a femoral hernia, then separated them. Cough impulse is shared, so lean on the fluid thrill and emptying on lying down.
You first put a venous ulcer at the toes, heel or lateral malleolus, then corrected. The venous ulcer follows pressure: gaiter area above the medial malleolus.
You first chose stockings for suitable symptomatic disease, then moved on. Stockings are for pregnancy, after treatment, or when intervention is unsuitable or declined.
You tend to answer with the old PYQ key or reject an accepted alternative. Learn both: the classic key and the current practice, then let the stem wording (current, first-line, classic) decide.
You tend to mismatch eponyms and associations: Perthes with Brodie-Trendelenburg, saphenous with sural nerve, the named perforators. Anchor each to what it does or accompanies, not to the name.

You tend to reverse a direction or mechanism: perforator flow, the calf pump, or what filling means on a tourniquet test. Before answering, state the normal direction first, then ask what disease reverses.

You tend to merge look-alikes: two Trendelenburgs, two saphenous veins, a varix and a hernia. Before answering, name the one feature that separates them, such as the noun after the eponym or the side of the malleolus.
You tend to miss the qualifier: stripping only to just below the knee, stockings only when intervention is unsuitable, foam for larger veins. Before answering, underline the limiting word.
You tend to get the order wrong or skip the first safety step: ABPI before compression, deep vein patency before stripping. Before acting, ask what must be confirmed first, and why.
You tapped Sure on at least two answers that were wrong. Those are the ones to fix first: confident errors, once corrected, stick best. Before tapping Sure, name the one fact that decides the answer.

You asked for hints or explanations often. Used well, that is a strategy. Next time, try to commit to an answer first, then check it; the review cards will show whether the ideas hold without support.

Start with the review cards for your gap objectives, in the order listed, beginning with any you were sure about but missed. Then redo the module in two or three days; a second pass with the corrected models is where this topic sticks.
